title: Kaikeyi's two wishes
hook: the maid Manthara; the old promise called in

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's swayamvara, a bow snapped and a garland placed. Sita-Ram, her name comes first. Today, years later in Ayodhya, a happy announcement goes wrong overnight.

Dasharatha is old now, and he makes the announcement the whole kingdom wants: tomorrow, Rama will be crowned as heir. The city goes wild. Flags, flowers, lamps in every window. In the palace, Queen Kaikeyi, Bharata's mother, hears the news and is delighted. She loves Rama. She even gives a jewel to the servant who brought the news: her old maid, Manthara, who came with her from her childhood home. Manthara throws the jewel down. Are you a fool? she says. When Rama is king, his mother will be queen mother, and you'll be her servant. And your son, Bharata, will have nothing.
screen: `TOMORROW, RAMA WILL BE CROWNED.` → `KAIKEYI IS DELIGHTED.` → `MANTHARA THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: At first Kaikeyi argues: Rama is good, Rama is fair. But Manthara keeps talking, all night, and slowly the fear gets in. Then Manthara reminds her of something. Long ago, in a battle, Dasharatha was wounded, and Kaikeyi saved his life. In gratitude he promised her two wishes, anything she asked, and she never used them. Use them now. So Kaikeyi goes to the room where a queen goes when she is angry, throws off her jewelry, and lies on the bare floor. Dasharatha finds her there, frantic. I'll give you anything. She makes him swear it, on Rama's name. Then she asks. First wish: crown Bharata instead. Second wish: send Rama into the forest, in exile, for fourteen years. He begs and pleads all night. But he gave his word, and he can't take it back. Why not? Because Hinduism counts truth, satya, as part of dharma, and a promise is a truth about the future. Tulsidas's retelling puts it in a line Hindu families still quote: in Rama's family, the custom has always been, let life go, but never the given word. Pran jaye par vachan na jaye. Who is to blame? The tradition argues. In Valmiki, Kaikeyi and Manthara make a real, human choice. In some later tellings, the gods send the goddess Saraswati to turn Manthara's mind. People still debate whether a promise pulled out like this should bind. But the story is clear about the teaching: a word given in gratitude, years ago, is still a word.
screen: `MANTHARA TALKS ALL NIGHT.` · `THE OLD PROMISE: TWO WISHES.` · `CROWN BHARATA. EXILE RAMA.` · `LET LIFE GO, NOT THE GIVEN WORD.` · then, large: `A GIVEN WORD IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise you've made that's still open, one you made easily that has since got heavy. If you pray, ask for the strength to keep it, or the honesty to talk about it. If you don't, just name it, and decide one small step toward keeping it.
Vara, a boon once granted and almost forgotten, called in at last: Bharata to be crowned, and Rama sent into the forest for fourteen years.
Your line: a given word is dharma. Even one given in gratitude, long ago. That's day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindus retell Kaikeyi's wishes as the turning point of the Ramayana; in Ramlila performances it's often the moment the audience goes quiet, and many discuss how much blame Kaikeyi and Manthara bear.
